terms.meaning: Key performance indicator, a number used to track how well the product is doing.
The share of users who come back a set number of days later, here day 7 and day 30.
The count that is being measured on top, and the count of everyone it could apply to on the bottom.
A record that a user did something in the app, such as viewing a moment or sharing.

sections.name: File setup, at, ev
sections.title: Sets up time and event helpers
sections.what: Defines helpers that turn a text date into a UTC time and build one analytics event with a user, name, properties and time.
sections.why: Likely reason: it keeps the long list of test events short and readable.
sections.watch_out: Times are read as UTC because the code adds a Z to the text. A time without a Z offset would be read the same way, so changes here shift every metric.

sections.name: EVENTS
sections.title: Fictional week of events
sections.what: Lists about two dozen fictional events for four users in one week, with a short note on each explaining why it matters for the expected answers.
sections.why: Likely reason: a small, hand-checked dataset makes each expected answer easy to verify.
sections.watch_out: Every expected answer depends on these exact events. Adding or moving one changes many tests at once.

sections.name: kpi: north star and weekly KPIs with known answers
sections.title: Checks weekly numbers by hand
sections.what: Checks the week starts on a Monday, four users were active, and the review-to-next-read ratio is one in three. Checks supporting ratios such as calls per fan, participation, first call for new fans, day 7 and day 30 retention, share rate and receipt tap-through. Checks that unknown values are shown as null, not zero, when there is no data or the retention window has not passed.
sections.why: Likely reason: a null value tells the team the data is not ready, while zero would look like a real drop.
sections.watch_out: Retention is only counted once its window has passed. A null value means not enough time has passed, not that retention is zero.

sections.name: kpi: computed from the event log
sections.title: Checks database numbers match the pure maths
sections.what: Clears the test database, loads the same events into it, and checks the service returns exactly the same weekly numbers as the pure calculation.
sections.why: Likely reason: the app reads numbers from the database, so this confirms the storage path gives the same answers as the calculation.
sections.watch_out: Leftover events from other tests would change the numbers, so the reset before loading must run.

summary: Tests the weekly product numbers (KPIs) for fans, such as active users, retention and share rate, against answers worked out by hand.
purpose: Makes sure the team's weekly health numbers are calculated correctly from the event log, and that missing data shows as unknown rather than zero.
why: Likely reason: the team makes decisions from these numbers, so wrong maths would mislead them. Reason not stated in the code for each specific metric.
how: Builds a small set of fictional events for four users over one week and writes the expected answers in comments. Checks the week start, the active user count, and each metric's numerator, denominator and value. Checks that metrics with no data or an unfinished window return null. Last, loads the same events into the database and checks the service returns the same numbers as the pure calculation.
inputs: A list of fictional analytics events with user ids, event names, properties and times, and the week start and end times.
outputs: Pass or fail results, and for the database test, rows written to the test database.
risks: Expected values depend on the exact events, so adding one changes many answers. The database test writes rows that must be cleared first.
debug: If a metric is wrong, find its test and compare the numerator and denominator with the hand-worked comment. Then check the pure weekly calculation for that metric.
